title: Who holds which key
scenario: The studio reviews how its keys and tokens are kept before it links more tools. You decide what to change. Use the exhibit. The sheet is made up for this case. The rules come from the docs.
exhibit:
KEY SHEET (made up for this case):
  K1  OpenAI model key. Typed into the script of the studio's public
      moodboard web page.
  K2  Gemini model key. A standard key with no restrictions. Pasted in the
      team chat last month.
  K3  Design-tool access. Each designer signs in with their own account.
  K4  Scheduler token. One admin token, entered once by the studio owner and
      used by every teammate's requests.
  K5  OpenAI project key "studio-all". One project serves both live client
      work and the team's tests.

questions.prompt: What is the best fix for K1, the OpenAI key in the moodboard page?

options.text: Hide the key by splitting it into two pieces inside the page's own script file
options.explanation: Anyone can still read both pieces in the browser. Keys in client-side code can be extracted.

options.text: Move the model calls to the studio's server, keep the key there, and replace the old key
options.explanation: Right. The Gemini API and OpenAI docs both say keys must not sit in client code. A backend server holds the key. A key that was exposed should be replaced.

options.text: Keep the key in the page, but tell the whole team never to share the web page address
options.explanation: A page address is easy to find. The key can be read by any visitor.

options.text: Keep the key in the page, and set a low spend limit so that any misuse stays cheap
options.explanation: A limit caps the damage but leaves the key exposed. Move it out of the page.

questions.prompt: K2 is a standard Gemini key with no restrictions, shared in chat. What do you do?

options.text: Nothing, because unrestricted keys are the type that Gemini wants every studio to use
options.explanation: The Gemini API docs say the Gemini API rejects requests from unrestricted standard keys.

options.text: Paste the key into the repository, so that there is one place where the team finds it
options.explanation: The Gemini API docs say never to check keys into source control.

options.text: Share the key with Client A too, so that the studio and client use the same single key
options.explanation: Sharing a key widens the reach of a leak. Keys should be kept apart.

options.text: Make a new key in AI Studio, an auth key by default, keep it out of chat, and retire K2
options.explanation: Right. The Gemini API docs say new AI Studio keys are auth keys, and unrestricted standard keys are rejected. A key pasted in chat is no longer private.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with K4, the one shared scheduler token?

options.text: Every request has one identity, so you cannot tell who posted, and it may give too much
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say a shared static credential carries the same key for all members and cannot tell users apart. Use OAuth to act as a person.

options.text: A shared token is slower than a personal one, so each post takes much longer to go out
options.explanation: The pages do not describe any speed cost. The issue is who is identified.

options.text: A token can only be used once, so the studio owner has to type it in again for each post
options.explanation: The page describes no such rule. A static credential is sent with every request.

options.text: The scheduler will not accept an admin token, since admins are not allowed to post at all
options.explanation: Nothing says so. The risk is the shared identity, not a ban on admins.

questions.prompt: K5 serves live client work and the team's tests in one project. What is the better set-up?

options.text: Keep one project, but ask testers to run their jobs only at night, when live work is quiet
options.explanation: Timing does not separate the keys or the limits. A test can still hit live limits and live data.

options.text: Keep one project, and watch the monthly bill so that the team can spot test spending late
options.explanation: Watching a bill is not a limit. The OpenAI docs describe limits that are set per project.

options.text: Separate staging and production projects, with custom rate and spend limits per project
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say you can create separate projects for staging and production, limit who can open production, and set custom rate and spend limits per project.

options.text: Give testers the production key, so that every test matches the live set-up exactly
options.explanation: This puts the live key in more hands. Tests should not carry production rights.
